activities.anchor: The airframe divides into three functional parts
activities.caption: pair each part with its job
activities.name: asiAirframeMatch

config.prompt: Three functional parts, two helpers — pair each with its job:

pairs.right: carries crew, payload and the tail
makes lift — spars carry bending, ribs hold shape, stressed skin shares the work
stability and fine control — vertical fin plus rudder, horizontal stabiliser plus elevator
trade drag for lift at low speed — the controllable approach
neutralise control pressure so the aircraft flies hands-off

config.why: The whole system is rigged so stability, not the pilot, is the first line of level flight — disturb a stable aircraft and it seeks to return itself.

activities.anchor: First, ignition: the spark comes from
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the mixture briefing
activities.name: asiMixtureSpot

config.prompt: This engine briefing contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Most trainers burn 100LL avgas in an air-cooled four-cylinder boxer engine turning a propeller at around 2,400 rpm.
The cycle is the familiar four-stroke: intake, compression, power, exhaust.
The mixture must be leaned in flight because air density falls with altitude.
Too rich a mixture burns pistons; too lean wastes fuel and fouls plugs.
On the ground, a hot day or high field elevation saps takeoff power the same way.
config.correction: Inverted: too RICH wastes fuel and fouls plugs; too LEAN burns pistons — the lean side is the dangerous one.
config.why: The mixture knob is a power-and-safety control: the engine breathes thinner air up high, so the fuel–air ratio follows it.

activities.caption: drag the divider — fixed versus constant-speed
activities.name: asiPropCompare

config.prompt: Two prop philosophies — drag between them:

before.label: Fixed-pitch prop
before.text: A compromise blade, best at one regime — the trainer's fitting: simple, rugged, adequate.

after.label: Constant-speed prop
after.text: Blade angle varies to keep the engine efficient across the whole envelope — the upgrade that separates trainers from touring aircraft.

config.why: The propeller is itself a rotating wing — so the prop choice is really a mission choice.

activities.anchor: the engine is the riskiest system in the aircraft
activities.caption: bet first — what actually downplanes trainers?
activities.name: asiRiskPredict

config.q: Which system causes most light-aircraft accidents?
choices: the engine — mechanical failure dominates accident statistics
decisions: fuel exhaustion, weather continued-into, manoeuvring low over the ground
the landing gear collapsing on touchdown
config.why: Modern aero engines are astonishingly reliable — most accidents are not mechanical at all. Systems knowledge is really decision knowledge: fuel selection, mixture, oil pressure are the pilot's to manage.

activities.anchor: The classic "six-pack" panel divides by sensor
activities.caption: file the instruments — which sensor feeds which dial?
activities.name: asiPanelBuckets

config.prompt: The six-pack divides by what each dial trusts — file them:

items.label: airspeed indicator — ram air minus static pressure
altimeter — an aneroid barometer calibrated to altitude
vertical speed indicator — how fast pressure is changing
heading indicator — realigned to the compass every so often
turn coordinator — rate and quality of turn
the magnetic compass — needs no power at all

config.why: Two pressure sensors feed three instruments; spinning gyros feed three more — knowing what each dial trusts is what lets you reason about what a stuck instrument will read.

activities.caption: pin the realignment interval on the clock
activities.name: asiGyroPlace

config.prompt: The gyroscopic heading indicator slowly precesses. About how often must it be realigned to the magnetic compass?
config.why: About every fifteen minutes — the gyro holds a steady reference the compass cannot, but precession creeps in, so the compass periodically re-truths it.
config.context: The compass swings in turns and accelerations; the gyro drifts in between — which is why the two are cross-checked rather than trusted alone.

activities.caption: true or false — the polite failure
activities.name: asiFailJudge

statements.s: Instruments fail politely and wrongly — a slowly winding-down gyro, an airspeed indicator drifting upward.
statements.why: The dangerous moment is never the failure itself but the pilot flying by an instrument that has quietly begun to lie.

statements.s: Instruments fail loudly, with a warning light for every fault.
statements.why: Some failures are engineered to indicate (low-vacuum, low-voltage), but the design assumes the residual failure will be silent.

statements.s: The defence is the cross-check: instruments are read as a set, and any single dissenter is suspect.
statements.why: Each confirming the others — which is why the training is so relentless.

statements.s: A pilot without outside references who trusts a lying instrument can enter a graveyard spiral within a minute.
statements.why: The attitude feels level, the circle tightens, the descent steepens — spatial disorientation is what instrument flying was invented to defeat.

activities.caption: rebuild the walkaround, cabin to pitot
activities.name: asiWalkOrder

config.prompt: The preflight that catches problems before they fly — put it in order:
items: in the cabin: documents (ARROW), controls and switches, fuel selector
fuel samples drained from sumps at each tank and the gascolator
oil quantity and security; propeller and spinner inspected for nicks
control surfaces moved through full travel — full and free
tyres, brakes, shock struts, antennas — and the pitot tube uncovered
config.why: The fuel sample is the single most important check — water sinks below the gasoline in the cup — and a pitot cover forgotten on the tube has quietly produced airspeed-zero takeoffs.
